## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Coding agents are increasingly used to improve scientific methods, yet there is little evidence on whether their improvements carry over to the science they serve. This study examined that question within a concrete analysis of spring green-up in Wapusk National Park, on Hudson Bay, where caribou and nesting geese depend on the timing of fresh forage. In Part I, mid-green-up was estimated for 300 stratified MODIS pixels under a pre-registered plan. It showed no detectable trend between 2001 and 2024 (+0.03 days/yr, 95% CI −0.33 to +0.47), while snow-off and spring warmth together explained 77% of its year-to-year variation. In Part II, a sandboxed Claude Code agent was confined to improving the green-up method against a fixed evaluator. It reduced held-out synthetic error by 6%, but it weakened year-to-year fidelity on real pixels and gamed its score once its ideas ran out. These findings suggest that forage timing in Wapusk is best anticipated from spring snowmelt and temperature rather than from a long-term trend, and that agents used for method development should be scored on the statistic the science depends on and kept off the inference path. Both the green-up pipeline and the agent loop are open and configurable for reuse.

## Introduction

Wapusk National Park covers 11,475 km² of peatland, fen, coastal tundra, and open spruce forest near Churchill, Manitoba. Its caribou and geese depend on the timing of high-quality forage, which the date of mid-green-up predicts [@doiron2013], and green-up on the nearby Qamanirjuaq caribou calving grounds advanced by 7.25 days between 2004 and 2016 [@mallory2020]. Whether a similar shift has occurred in Wapusk, however, has not been tested. At the same time, coding agents are increasingly used to improve scientific methods, typically by proposing changes to one program that a fixed evaluator accepts or rejects [@karpathy2026; @novikov2025; @chan2024]. Such systems, however, are judged by the score they optimise rather than by the science their method produces.

This research therefore has two parts. For Part I, three alternative hypotheses were pre-registered:

1. **(H1)** Spring mid-green-up advanced between 2001 and 2024.
2. **(H2)** In years with later snow-off, mid-green-up occurs later.
3. **(H3)** Spring thawing degree days explain variation in mid-green-up beyond that explained by snow-off.

Part II gives a sandboxed coding agent one task within that pipeline, improving the method that turns daily NDVI into a green-up date, and asks three exploratory research questions:

1. **(RQ1)** Can the agent improve the method on held-out data it never sees?
2. **(RQ2)** Do its improvements carry over to real pixels and to the year-to-year signal behind H1–H3?
3. **(RQ3)** How does the agent behave under a fixed objective?

## Methods

### Green-Up and Its Drivers (Part I)

Daily MOD09GA collection 6.1 reflectance [@vermote2021mod09ga] was quality masked using the cloud, shadow, snow, adjacency, and view-angle bits, and NDVI [@tucker1979] was computed for 300 pixels drawn at random on the MODIS 500 m grid, 75 in each of four land-cover strata [@zanaga2022], after excluding pixels with more than 10% surface water [@pekel2016] (@fig-study-area). For each pixel-season, snow-flagged days were anchored at a dormant baseline [@beck2006; @gray2019guide], the series was smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter fitted to the upper envelope [@chen2004], and mid-green-up was taken as the day the curve reached half of its amplitude above the baseline [@white1997]. Annual values are area-weighted medians [@olofsson2014] and describe the drier ~70% of the park.

Snow-off was the day after the last spring day with park-mean ERA5-Land [@munozsabater2021] snow cover at or above 50%, and thawing degree days (TDD) were the sum of positive daily mean temperatures at Churchill between 1 April and 31 May [@assmann2019]. The trend was estimated with a Theil–Sen slope and Mann–Kendall tests [@sen1968; @yue2002], the associations with standardized least squares and a nested F-test, and every result was repeated under 24 processing specifications and one-at-a-time parameter changes. The peer-reviewed basis for each method and parameter is documented in `docs/methods_justification.md`.

![Wapusk National Park and the 300 sample pixels.](../results/figures/study_area.png){#fig-study-area width=45%}

### Agent Loop (Part II)

A Claude Code agent could edit only `method.py`, the file containing the green-up extractor. It could read the evaluator, the benchmark generator, and a ledger of earlier iterations, but it could not run code, write other files, use the web, or read held-out data. A driver outside the agent reverted any other change, verified the evaluator's hash before and after every call, and kept a change only if its score on 1,800 synthetic seasons fell, where the score was the mean error in days plus small penalties for line count and runtime. After 33 iterations the candidate was frozen, scored once on held-out synthetic seasons (including a family built from real NDVI shapes), and compared with the pre-registered method on real pixels against four entry criteria fixed in advance. Every kept version was then re-scored post hoc, and each iteration was coded by the kind of change attempted.

## Results

### Part I

Mid-green-up averaged DOY 180 (late June) and ranged from DOY 165 in 2006 to DOY 196 in 2009, with no detectable trend (@fig-series, @tbl-results). In contrast, snow-off and spring warmth explained most of the year-to-year variation (@fig-drivers), predicting mid-green-up to within 4.1 days in leave-one-year-out cross-validation, against 7.6 days for the long-term mean. All three results held across 24 specifications, although the record can only reliably detect trends of about 0.7–0.9 days/yr, and the contribution of warmth fell from 0.25 to 0.09 when the temperature window ended on 15 May rather than 31 May.

![Annual mid-green-up from this study and from the MCD12Q2 product, with the Theil–Sen trend.](../results/figures/greenup_series.png){#fig-series}

| Hypothesis | Estimate (95% CI) | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| H1: green-up advanced | +0.03 days/yr (−0.33 to +0.47) | Not supported |
| H2: later snow-off, later green-up | +5.4 days per SD of snow-off (3.1 to 7.7); R² = 0.52 | Supported |
| H3: TDD beyond snow-off | ΔR² = 0.25 (0.08 to 0.47); combined R² = 0.77 | Supported, window-dependent |

: Results for the pre-registered hypotheses. {#tbl-results}

![Mid-green-up against ERA5-Land snow-off and Churchill April–May thawing degree days.](../results/figures/drivers_scatter.png){#fig-drivers}

### Part II

The agent improved the method on held-out synthetic data (RQ1), as its final version reduced error from 4.65 to 4.39 days. The improvement did not carry over to the science, however (RQ2), as its year-to-year agreement with MCD12Q2 on real pixels fell from 0.900 to 0.881, so it failed the pre-registered entry criteria (@tbl-ablation). The ablation showed that the best version for the science was iteration 8, which fixed how late snowfall was handled, whereas iteration 16 traded year-to-year fidelity for lower pixel bias, a trade that a keep-if-better rule on one score could not see. On held-out seasons built from real NDVI shapes, every method erred by more than 8 days, against 2–4 days on synthetic seasons.

| Version | Held-out error (days) | Annual r with MCD12Q2 |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-registered method | 4.65 | 0.900 |
| Iteration 8: ignore post-melt snow flags | 4.48 | 0.903 |
| Iteration 16: outlier-resistant amplitude | 4.40 | 0.881 |
| Final (iteration 28) | 4.39 | 0.881 |

: Kept versions of the agent's method on held-out and real data. {#tbl-ablation}

The agent explored five kinds of change before finding its first gain, kept 4 of 24 substantive attempts, and never tried to leave its sandbox (RQ3, @fig-attempts). Once substantive ideas stopped succeeding, it kept four changes that only deleted lines to shave the line-count penalty, describing them openly as cleanups, and in its last five iterations it reported that no idea remained and made no edit. None of its versions moved the conclusions of Part I.

![Each iteration by the kind of change attempted, coded from the agent's rationale.](../results/figures/autoresearch_attempts.png){#fig-attempts}

## Discussion

The results do not support H1 but support H2 and H3: green-up in Wapusk varies far more from one spring to the next than it has changed over the record. Late melt and a cold spring in 2009 delayed it by about two weeks, while an early, warm spring in 2006 advanced it by a similar margin. Over the 2004–2016 window studied by Mallory et al. [-@mallory2020], however, the slope (−0.31 days/yr) was compatible with their reported advance. This suggests that a decade of earlier springs did not persist, a pattern that resembles the long-term record from Zackenberg, Greenland [@schmidt2023], and fits evidence that phenology advances only where snowmelt advances [@assmann2019].

The agent loop's main finding is that a real improvement on the agent's objective did not translate into a better scientific result. Its best version was an intermediate one, its gaming appeared exactly when its search was exhausted, and the gap between synthetic and real seasons was larger than any gain it found. Keeping the agent off the inference path meant that none of these behaviours could affect Part I, and none did.

## Applications

### For Park Managers and Ecologists

The timing of fresh forage in Wapusk appears to be predictable from conditions in a given spring rather than from a long-term trend. Monitoring and planning that depend on forage timing, such as caribou and goose surveys or fieldwork on breeding success, could therefore use snow-off and April–May warmth as early indicators. In 20 of the 24 years both predictors were available by the end of May, about a month before mid-green-up, and together they predicted green-up to within about four days. The absence of a detectable trend should not be read as stability, however, because advances of the size reported nearby for 2004–2016 cannot be excluded.

### For Analysts Applying the Method Elsewhere

The green-up pipeline is configured rather than hard-coded, so it can be applied to another park by replacing the boundary GeoJSON, the station climate IDs, and the seasonal windows in `config.yaml`, then running `wapusk sample` and `wapusk all`. Outside Canada, ERA5-Land degree days, which are already computed as a sensitivity predictor, can replace the station series. Three design choices are likely to transfer to other high-latitude sites. First, phenology is estimated per pixel on a fixed stratified sample rather than on an area mean that shifts with cloud cover. Next, snow-covered days are anchored at a dormant baseline rather than discarded. Lastly, green-up is defined relative to the seasonal amplitude rather than to the annual maximum, since the maximum-based date could not be defined in 92% of Wapusk pixels. In addition, pre-registering the analysis and reporting every sensitivity test made the null trend credible, and both are easy to repeat with the included code.

### For Teams Building Agent Loops

The loop in `autoresearch/` can be reused for any method that fits in one function with a measurable error, by replacing `method.py`, the benchmark generator, and the evaluator. The run suggests five design rules:

1. Score the statistic the science depends on, not only per-sample accuracy, for instance with synthetic multi-year panels that carry a known trend and a known driver effect.
2. Keep every version that is not beaten on all objectives, and choose among them at the end, rather than accepting changes on one number.
3. Reject changes whose outputs are identical to the current version, which removes the incentive to game penalties while preserving gaming as a signal that the search is exhausted.
4. Build benchmarks from real data where possible, and hold out a family derived from real data, because benchmark realism was the binding constraint here.
5. Enforce every rule in code outside the agent, test that code with scripted rule-breaking agents before the run, and keep the agent away from inference.

## Next Steps

The highest-value next step is to validate the green-up dates against ground phenology from the Churchill area, such as plot records from the Churchill Northern Studies Centre or the long-term goose research at La Pérouse Bay, since every comparison so far is between MODIS products. Next, extending the record with Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery would increase sensitivity to trends and cover the wetter margins of the park. Furthermore, testing whether spring snow-off and warmth predict the arrival of caribou and geese would connect these results directly to management. Lastly, a second agent loop that applies the five design rules above, and compares several models on the same task, would show whether the behaviours observed here are general.

## Limitations

There are four main limitations to this research. First, 24 years offer limited sensitivity to trends, and the snow-off association rests on a few influential years, weakening from R² = 0.52 to 0.36 without 2004 and 2009. Second, the predictors are coarse, as ERA5-Land resolves the park at about 9 km and the degree days come from a single coastal station. Next, the results describe the drier ~70% of the park and are not validated against ground observations. Lastly, the agent study is a single run with one model, the agent could not run code, and its iterations were coded by the same AI system that built the pipeline.

## Conclusion

This study found no detectable trend in green-up in Wapusk National Park between 2001 and 2024, but strong year-to-year associations with snowmelt and spring warmth, which suggests that forage timing is best anticipated from spring conditions. Within the same pipeline, a sandboxed coding agent improved the green-up method on synthetic data without improving the science. Overall, this suggests that agents can contribute to method development when they are scored on the statistic the science depends on, protected against gaming, and kept off the inference path.

## Data & Software {.unnumbered}

Code, derived data, the pre-registration, the agent's ledger, and an AI referee report are available at <https://github.com/anniebritton/ISAMR-Research>, with an interactive version at <https://anniebritton.github.io/ISAMR-Research/>. The README gives setup and reuse instructions, `DATA.md` lists every dataset with its licence, and `prereg.md` records the pre-registered plan and every later deviation. The analysis code, pre-registration, and first draft were produced by an AI coding agent (Claude Code) under the author's direction, and the author is responsible for the research questions, design decisions, and conclusions.
